sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
An over 1000 km-long contraction belt runs along the eastern margin of the Adriatic Sea from the Alpine domain (to the North) to the Kefallonia-Lefkada Fault (to the south).
The various part of this fold and thrust belt are known, from north to south, as Dinarides, Albanides and Hellenides and result from the convergence between the European and African plates.
Along this margin the SW-NE convergence between the two plates has a strain rate of ~30 nanostrain/y (Hollenstein et al., 2003; Serpelloni et al., 2005).
Seismicity mostly concentrates in the Albanides and Hellenides. The outer portion of these chains is partly located offshore and characterized by a number of thrust fronts that seems to be contemporaneously active. The available focal mechanisms indicate a SW-NE maximum horizontal stress axis (Papazachos et al., 1999); reverse faulting dominates, even if some smaller strike-slip events are also present (Vannucci et al., 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006).
We propose that this Source be on the main of the thrust fronts that characterize the continental collision between the African and European plates, at a depth that ranges from 3 to 15 km.
This Source is presently characterized by shallow seismicity and several strong events (up to M=7.2) known from historical catalogues.
Average strike and rake computed by Papazachos et al. (1999) from focal mechanisms are consistent with plate motion vectors derived from GPS data and the orientation of the thrust front reported by many authors. We inferred dip from focal mechanisms available in literature and from the average dip of the thrust faults detected on seismic profiles acquired for hydrocarbon exploration (e.g. Picha, 2002).
We used GPS data to estimate the slip rate of this Source.
We adopted as maximum magnitude of this source the value assigned in the seismic zonation by Aliaj et al. (2004) to the Lezha-Ulqini Source Zone, which includes the most part of this Source.

evidence: Inferred from regional geological and seismological data.

pictures.t: Tectonic map of central and southern Adriatic regions.
pictures.c: Tectonic map of the southern part of the Dinarides and northern Albanides (from Picha, 2002).
These profiles show the tectonic style of the Albanides fold-and-thrust belt in the Montenegro area (from Picha [2002]).

pictures.t: Moment tensor solution for the Adriatic Sea and surrounding regions
pictures.c: This map shows that moment tensor solutions for the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea indicate mainly reverse faulting (from Pondrelli et al. [2006]).

pictures.t: Seismicity of map Albania and adjacent regions
pictures.c: The Northern Albania and Southern Albania offshore source areas fall in the region named PL (Periadriatic Lowland) and IC (Ionian Coast), respectively (from Aliaj et al. [2004]).
Parameters of the ten seismic source zones proposed by Aliaj et al. [2004] for Albania (from Aliaj et al. [2004]).

pictures.t: Stress field map of the Aegean region and surroundings
pictures.c: This map shows the horizontal compression and tension axes all over the Aegean and surrounding regions. The stress axes adopted for the Southern Albania offshore source area are marked as A3 (from Papazachos et al. [1999]).

pictures.t: Long-term fault slip rates for the External Dinarides
pictures.c: Average long-term fault slip rates for the External Dinarides (Kastelic and Carafa, 2012). The width of each colored band is proportional to long-term slip rate. The blue and green bands represent thrust and dextral strike-slip faulting, respectively. The numerical values plotted above the fault traces are the average slip rates for each fault element. Each active fault is coded with its corresponding alphanumeric value.
1979 seismic sequences activated almost an entire dimension of the active fault corresponding to the Montenegro offshore seismogenic source (after Benetatos and Kiratzi, 2006).
